analysis.research_question_and_background: Background Bangladesh experienced a major measles resurgence in 2026.
analysis.study_design_and_population: We reassessed early outbreak indicators while distinguishing daily notifications, cumulative burden and historical vaccination measures.
analysis.methods: Methods We conducted a descriptive analysis of Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) bulletins dated 2–30 April 2026, reporting cumulative totals from 15 March.
analysis.main_results: Results By 30 April, DGHS reported 37,131 suspected and 5,028 confirmed cases, with 227 suspected and 49 confirmed deaths.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Conclusions The early outbreak showed substantial reported burden and geographic heterogeneity.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: Accurate interpretation requires matching reporting windows, strengthening age- and vaccination-status surveillance and avoiding causal inferences from historical aggregate coverage.

analysis.summary_en: This study examines the measles resurgence in Bangladesh during 2026, focusing on the national surveillance trends, cumulative divisional burden, and historical vaccination context. The research aimed to reassess early outbreak indicators by distinguishing daily notifications, cumulative burden, and historical vaccination measures. A descriptive analysis of Directorate General of Health Services bulletins from 2–30 April 2026 was conducted, reporting cumulative totals from 15 March. By 30 April, 37,131 suspected and 5,028 confirmed measles cases were reported, with 227 suspected and 49 confirmed deaths. The study highlights the substantial reported burden and geographic heterogeneity of the early outbreak. The findings emphasize the need for accurate interpretation by aligning reporting windows, enhancing age- and vaccination-status surveillance, and avoiding causal inferences from historical aggregate coverage. The study's limitations include the lack of contemporaneous MR1 measurements for correlation testing, which affects the strength of the evidence.

title: Susceptibility-weighted imaging findings in subacute sclerosing panencephalitis: subcortical paramagnetic rim and deep gray matter changes.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder caused by persistent measles virus infection. Conventional MRI plays a key role in diagnosis and staging; however, susceptibility-weighted imaging (SWI) findings in SSPE have not been systematically characterized, particularly with respect to their relationship to disease burden and neurodegeneration.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This retrospective single-center study included 126 patients with confirmed SSPE who underwent MRI including SWI.
analysis.methods: T2/FLAIR hyperintensities were assessed across predefined supratentorial and infratentorial parenchymal regions. A composite total parenchymal disease burden score was calculated. Cerebral atrophy and deep gray matter mineralization were evaluated using semi-quantitative visual grading systems. SWI was also assessed for the presence of a SPR. Associations between susceptibility findings, parenchymal disease burden, cerebral atrophy, and clinical parameters were analyzed using non-parametric statistical methods.
analysis.main_results: SPR was identified in 14 of 128 MRI studies (10.9%), most commonly involving the parietal lobes. Patients with the rim had significantly longer symptom duration, higher disease stage, greater parenchymal disease burden, higher atrophy scores, and higher deep gray matter mineralization scores compared with patients without the rim (p < 0.01). Deep gray matter mineralization scores showed significant positive correlations with both global parenchymal disease burden and cerebral atrophy (Spearman's ρ, p < 0.001).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: SPR and deep gray matter mineralization are associated with increasing parenchymal disease burden and atrophy. These findings likely represent imaging markers of disease chronicity and provide complementary information to conventional MRI, particularly in the evaluation of chronic encephalitis in measles-endemic regions.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings provide complementary information to conventional MRI, particularly in the evaluation of chronic encephalitis in measles-endemic regions. They may inform the development of more accurate imaging-based diagnostic and staging tools for SSPE.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is retrospective and based on a single-center cohort, which may limit generalizability. The evidence is moderate due to the observational nature of the study and the reliance on semi-quantitative visual grading systems.

analysis.summary_en: This study aimed to evaluate susceptibility-weighted imaging (SWI) changes in subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE), focusing on the Subcortical Paramagnetic Rim (SPR) and deep gray matter mineralization. It included 126 patients with confirmed SSPE who underwent MRI. The methods involved assessing T2/FLAIR hyperintensities, calculating a composite disease burden score, and evaluating cerebral atrophy and mineralization using visual grading systems. The main results showed that SPR was identified in 10.9% of cases, with patients exhibiting the rim having significantly longer symptom duration, higher disease stage, and greater parenchymal disease burden. Deep gray matter mineralization scores correlated with disease burden and atrophy. The authors interpreted these findings as imaging markers of disease chronicity, offering complementary information to conventional MRI. The study's significance lies in its potential to improve diagnostic and staging tools for SSPE in measles-endemic regions. However, the limitations include the retrospective design and single-center setting, which may affect generalizability.

title: Comparative Modeling of Measles Incidences Among Children Below Five Years in Rivers State, Nigeria Using the Holt-Winters, SARIMA, and Hybrid SARIMA-ANN Models

analysis.research_question_and_background: This research analyzed various time-series forecasting models for measles occurrences in children younger than five in Rivers State, Nigeria, utilizing monthly data sourced from the Rivers State Hospital Management Board and allied partners spanning from January 2015 to December 2024. The study aimed to assess the prediction efficacy of additive Holt–Winters, multiplicative Holt–Winters, Seasonal Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average (SARIMA), and hybrid SARIMA–Artificial Neural Network (ANN) models.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The investigation focused on the temporal patterns of measles cases and assessed the prediction efficacy of four models using monthly data from January 2015 to December 2024. Python 3.11 software was used for the data analysis.
analysis.methods: The data series was explored using descriptive statistics, seasonal decomposition, the Jarque–Bera normality examination, the Augmented Dickey–Fuller unit-root evaluation, autocorrelation assessment, and the Ljung–Box test. Forecasting efficiency was measured via root mean squared error (RMSE), mean absolute scaled error (MASE), and mean absolute percentage error (MAPE).
analysis.main_results: The data series displayed positive skewness and did not conform to a normal distribution. The Augmented Dickey–Fuller test suggested stationarity at level significance (p < 0.001). The Ljung–Box analysis uncovered significant serial correlations at lags 12 and 20 (p < 0.001). The multiplicative Holt–Winters method yielded the best results, achieving the lowest RMSE at 16.43 and a reported MASE of 86.68, while the hybrid SARIMA–ANN approach was the least effective, presenting an RMSE of 22.05 and a reported MASE of 261.66.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study concludes that the multiplicative Holt–Winters method stands out as the most effective model among those tested. It suggests the validation of the reported MASE values, the importance of consistent out-of-sample evaluation, and enhancing regular measles monitoring to aid in timely forecasting, vaccination strategy, and focused public health actions.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings can inform the development of more accurate forecasting models for measles, which can aid in timely vaccination strategies and public health interventions. The study highlights the need for consistent out-of-sample evaluation and regular monitoring of measles cases.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study's findings are based on a specific dataset and may not be generalizable to other regions or populations.

analysis.summary_en: This study analyzed various time-series forecasting models for measles occurrences in children younger than five in Rivers State, Nigeria, using monthly data from 2015 to 2024. The multiplicative Holt–Winters method was found to be the most effective model, with implications for improving measles monitoring and vaccination strategies.

title: The effect of age at first dose of a measles-containing vaccine on measles humoral immunity: a retrospective cohort study, Canada, 2014 to 2016

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to estimate the effect of age at first dose of measles-containing vaccine (MCV1) on measles IgG concentration and seronegativity among two-dose recipients nearly two decades after vaccination. analysis.study_design_and_population: A retrospective cohort study was conducted of 10,766 twice-vaccinated individuals tested for measles IgG from 2014 to 2016 in Ontario, Canada. The study focused on females vaccinated with MCV1 at 12 to 15 months of age.
analysis.methods: The study used a retrospective cohort design to predict measles IgG concentration and seronegativity based on age at first dose of MCV1. It analyzed data from individuals tested for measles IgG between 2014 and 2016 in Ontario, Canada.
analysis.main_results: A 1-month increase in age at MCV1 (between 12 and 15 months) was associated with 13.7% (95% confidence interval (CI): 7.1–20.8) higher predicted mean measles IgG concentration for females born after elimination and 9.2% (95% CI: 6.8–11.6) for females born before elimination. Depending on the seronegativity threshold and the measles elimination status at birth, a 1-month increase in age at MCV1 was associated with lower odds ratios of seronegativity ranging from 0.74 (95% CI: 0.63–0.85) to 0.87 (95% CI: 0.57–1.27).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors suggest that delaying MCV1 to older ages (13–15 months) may result in an absolute decrease as large as 6% in the percentage of seronegative individuals, potentially increasing the likelihood of maintaining herd immunity.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings may inform strategies for measles vaccination programs, particularly regarding optimal timing of the first dose to ensure adequate humoral immunity and reduce the risk of seronegativity in the long term.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is based on retrospective data and may be subject to biases inherent in such designs. The evidence is moderate as it relies on statistical predictions rather than direct experimental validation.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated the effect of age at first dose of measles-containing vaccine (MCV1) on measles humoral immunity in Canada, focusing on females vaccinated between 12 and 15 months of age. Retrospective data from 10,766 twice-vaccinated individuals tested for measles IgG between 2014 and 2016 were analyzed. Results showed that a 1-month increase in age at MCV1 was associated with higher predicted IgG concentrations and lower odds of seronegativity, depending on the threshold and elimination status at birth. Using the lowest threshold and longest follow-up, 4.1% of females vaccinated at 15 months were predicted to be seronegative, compared with 9.6% of those vaccinated at 12 months. The authors suggest that delaying MCV1 may reduce seronegativity and help maintain herd immunity. The study's findings are of moderate strength due to its retrospective design and reliance on statistical predictions.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to compare national and sub-national childhood vaccination coverage estimates from Kenya's facility-based Health Information System (KHIS) and the 2022 Kenya Demographic Health Survey (KDHS) to assess concordance between the two data sources and to evaluate the suitability of routine data for programmatic decision-making. title: A multi-region discrete time chain binomial model for infectious disease transmission

analysis.research_question_and_background: Conventional mathematical models of infectious diseases often overlook the spatial spread of the disease, focusing only on local transmission. However, spatial propagation of various diseases has been observed mainly due to the movement of infectious individuals from one region to another.
analysis.study_design_and_population: In this work, we propose a multiregion discrete-time chain binomial framework to model dependencies between infection time series from neighboring regions.
analysis.methods: The proposed model is based on the epidemiological principle that new infections arise from interactions between susceptible and previously infected individuals. To strengthen the statistical formulation, the probability of new infections within each spatial unit is modeled through a link function, by allowing it to depend on lagged local incidence, inter-regional transmission effects, and region-specific covariates. To reduce complexity of the model as the number of regions increases, sparsity is imposed by using spatial contiguity matrices and k-nearest-neighbor structures. For estimating these multiregion models, an appropriate likelihood function maximization approach is proposed.
analysis.main_results: In-depth analyses of two real measles datasets and simulation studies incorporating seasonal patterns, different weight matrices across connected regions, and varying intervention strategies are used to motivate the proposed modeling framework and demonstrate its ability to reproduce realistic outbreak dynamics. While the simulation studies demonstrate applicability of the general AR(p) approach, the real data analysis of measles shows that an AR(1) model is adequate to capture the temporal dependence.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The framework allows for higher-order temporal dependence through an AR(p) specification and reduces complexity of the model as the number of regions increases by using sparsity.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The framework can reproduce realistic outbreak dynamics and is useful for forecasting disease counts in connected spatial units. It is particularly relevant for understanding and predicting the spread of measles in different regions.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The proposed model relies on the assumption that new infections arise from interactions between susceptible and previously infected individuals. The real data analysis of measles shows that an AR(1) model is adequate to capture the temporal dependence, but the model's performance may be limited by the complexity of real-world transmission dynamics.

analysis.summary_en: This study proposes a multiregion discrete-time chain binomial model to better understand and predict the spatial spread of infectious diseases, particularly measles. The model incorporates lagged local incidence, inter-regional transmission effects, and region-specific covariates to capture temporal dependencies and reduce complexity.
